རྣམས་ནི་རིམ་པ་བཞིན་དོན་བཞི་བཞི་ལ་དབང་མྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། མིག་རྣ་དག་ནི་ལུས་མཛེས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་ལུས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྲུང་བ་དང་། མཚུངས་ལྡན་དང་བཅས་པའི་རྣམ་ཤེས་སྐྱེད་པ་དང་། གཟུང་བ་ལྟ་བ་དང་སྒྲ་མཉན་པ་དག་གི་མཐུན་མོང་མིན་པའི་རྡུལ་དབང་མྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར།
དང་པོ་གྲུབ་སྟེ་། མིག་རྣའི་དབང་པོ་མེད་པའི་ལོང་བ་དང་འོན་པ་དག་མི་མཛེས་པའི་ཕྱིར། གཉིས་པ་གྲུབ་སྟེ་། མིག་གིས་གཡང་ས་ལ་སོཌ་པ་མཐོང་བ་དང་རྣ་བས་སྟག་གི་སྒྲ་ལ་སོཌ་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ཡ་ང་བས་སྤང་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། གསུཾ་པ་དང་བཞི་པ་གྲུབ་སྟེ། དབང་པོའི་ཡུལ་ལ
སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ་ཤིས་པ་སྐྱེ་བ་དབང་ཡུལ་གཉིས་ཀ་ལ་ལྟོས་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོར་དབང་པོས་སྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། མིག་གིས་ཉན་པ་དང་རྣ་བས་མཐོང་བ་སོཌ་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སྣ་ལྕེ་ལུས་རྣམས་ནི་རྟེན་མཛེས་པ་དང་ལུས་བསྲུང་བ་དང་རྣམ་ཤེས་མཚུངས་ལྡན་བཅས་སྐྱེད་
པ་དང་རྗེ་བསྣམ་པར་མྱང་བ་རེག་བྱ་རེག་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཆུ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་དེ། དེ་རྣམས་ཉམས་ན་མི་མཛེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཁམ་ཟས་ལ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་པས་ལུས་སྲུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ་གཞན་དག་མཚུངས་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །ཕོ་མ་སྲོག་ཡིད་ཀྱི་དབང་པོ་
རྣམས་ནི་རེ་རེ་ཞིང་དོན་གཉིས་གཉིས་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་དེ། རེ་ཞིག་ཕོ་མོའི་དབང་པོ་དག་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་དང་ཁྱད་པར་དག་ལ་དབང་མྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། བསྐལ་པ་འདི་ཚང་པའི་དང་པོར་ཕོ་མོའི་དབང་པོ་དག་མ་བྱུང་བའི་ཆོ་ག་འུ་དེ་དག་གི་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་བལ་ཕོ་མོའི་དབང་
བྱུང་ནས་ཕོ་མོའི་མིང་གི་བྱེ་བྲག་དང་དབྱིབས་དང་རོ་སོཌ་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡང་བྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར། ཁ་གཅིག་དབང་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཉོན་དང་རྣམ་གྲང་ལའང་དབང་བར་འདོད་དེ། དབང་པོ་དེ་དག་མེད་པའི་ཟ་མ་དང་དབང་པོ་ཉམས་པའི་མ་ནིང་ཕྲག་དོག་ཅན་སོཌ་བཞི་པོ་རྣམས་ལ་སྡོམ་མིན
དང་མཚམས་མེད་དང་དགེ་བ་ཆད་པ་རྣམས་མེད་ཅིང་། སྡོམ་པ་དང་སྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པ་དང་ཆ་བྲལ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་མེད་ལ། ཕོ་མོའི་དབང་པོ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ལ་སྡེ་ཚན་སྔ་ཕྱི་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་ཟེར་རོ།། སྲོག་གི་དབང་པོ་ནི་རིས་མཐུན་པར་མཚམས་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་ཡང་དག་པར་འཛིན
གཉིས་ལ་དབང་གྱུར་ཏེ། ཚེ་སྲིད་གྱི་མཇུག་ཐོག་ཏུ་སྲིད་པ་བར་དོ་ལ་གཟུང་མེད་དུ་སྐྱེ་བའི་སྲིད་པར་མཚམས་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཚེ་སྲོག་རྙེད་པས་དེར་དབང་བར་གྲུབ་ཅིང་། དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་སྲིད་པ་དེ་མ་འཕོས་ཀྱི་བར་དུ་ཡང་དག་པར་འཛིན་ཅིང་གནས་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་དབང་བར་གྲུབ

གཟུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཡིད་བདེ་ལས་ངེས་འདུད་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡིད་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཡིད་བདེ་བས་ངེས་འདུད་སྐྱེ་བའི་བར་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་དང་། བཏང་སྙོམས་གང་ཀྱང་བསྡུས་ནས་བསྟེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡིད་བདེ་སོང་གསུཾ་ཡང་རྣཾ་གྲང་ལ་དབང་བ་ཡོད་པར་འདོད་དོ།། འདིར་མདོ་སྡེ་པའི་བྱ་བྲག་དཔེ་སྟན་པ་དག་གིས་
བྱ་སྨྲས་ཤིག་རྣ་དག་གིས་ལུས་སྲུང་བར་འདོད་པ་མི་ཟད་དེ། མིག་གིས་འཇོ་པ་མཐོང་བ་དང་རྣ་བས་འཇོ་པའི་སྦོབས་པ་ཙཾ་ཁོ་ནས་ལུས་སྲུང་བ་མི་ནུས་པ་གང་ཞིག། དེར་ཡིད་ཀྱི་རྣཾ་ཤེས་མཚུངས་ལྡན་དང་བཅས་པས་འཇིཌ་པ་དེ་ཤེས་ནས་སྤོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། དབང་བས་ལུས་ལུས་མཛེས་པ་ལ
དབང་བར་འདོད་པའང་མི་ཟད་དེ། དབང་པོ་དང་བཅས་པའི་དབང་རྟེན་ཎ་ནས་མཛེས་པར་བྱེད་པ་གང་ཞིག། དབང་པོ་རྣཾས་ནི་དབང་པོའི་ཡུལ་ལས་འདས་པས་མཛེས་པར་བྱེད་པ་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ།། དེས་ན་བྱེ་སྨྲའི་འདོད་པ་ལས་དབང་ལྔས་རྣཾ་ཤེས་མཚུངས་ལྡན་བཅས་སྐྱེད་
པས་དབང་བ་ཁོ་ན་འཐད་ཅིང་གཞན་གར་སྨྲས་པ་རྣཾས་མི་འདོད་པ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་པའི་ལུགས་སོ།། །།གཉིས་པ་མདོ་སྡེ་པའི་ལུང་ནི། རང་གི་དོན་དང་ཐཾད་ལ།། དམིཌ་པར་དབང་བྱེད་ཕྱིར་དབང་།། །།མཉཾ་པ་ཀྱི་དབང་བ་འགྱུར་རོ།། ལུས་ལས་མ་དང་པདྨ་དབང་དག། རས་གནས་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་
དང་།། རྣཾ་པར་གྲངས་དབང་བྱེད་ཕྱིརོ།། སྲོག་དང་ཚར་བ་རྣཾས་དང་ནི།། དད་པ་དབང་བ་སྔར་འདོད་དག། མྱ་ངན་འདས་སོ་གང་ནས་གང་།། ཐོབ་པ་ལ་ནི་དབང་བྱེད་ཕྱིར།། ཀུན་ཤེས་བྱེད་དང་ཀུན་ཤེས་དང་།། དེ་བཞིན་ཀུན་ཤེས་ལྡན་དབང་པོ།། ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། བྱེ་སྨྲའི་འདོད་པ་དེ་རྣཾས་ལ་ཞེས་པའི་ཚིག་གིས་ཕལ་ཆེར་
མི་ཐད་པར་བསྟན་ན་ཁྱེད་རང་གི་འདོད་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། མིག་ནས་ཡིད་ཀྱི་བར་དབང་པོ་ཉུག་པ་དེ་དག་ལས་མིག་སོཌ་ལུས་ནི་རང་རང་གི་དོན་གཟུངས་ལྔ་པོ་དམིཌ་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་དེ། དབང་པོ་ལྔ་པོ་མེད་པར་གཟུངས་ལ་ལྷུག་པར་དམིཌ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། མི་སང་ནི
གཟུངས་སུ་དམིཌ་པའི་རྒྱུན་ཡོད་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཡིད་དབང་ནི་གཟུང་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བར་དོན་ཐཾད་ལ་དམིཌ་པ་ལ་དབང་བྱེད་དེ། ཡིད་ཀྱི་དབང་པོ་དེ་ཡུལ་ཐཾད་ལ་དམིཌ་པས་འཇུག་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། འདིར་གཟུངས་ཀྱང་དམིཌ་པ་ལ་དབང་བར་ཐལ། གཟུངས་དང་དོན་མེད་ན་དེའི་དམིཌ་པ་མི་

...the faculties are respectively without power over four purposes each. The eye and ear do not exercise power over making the body beautiful, protecting the body, producing consciousness together with its concordant factors, and the unique particles of seeing the visible and hearing the sound. The first is established because the blind and the deaf, who lack the eye and ear faculties, are not beautiful. The second is established because by seeing a precipice etc. with the eyes and hearing the sound of a tiger etc. with the ears, one avoids them out of fear. The third and fourth are established because when experiencing the objects of the faculties, although the birth of cognition depends on both the faculty and the object, it is primarily produced by the faculty; and it is impossible to hear with the eye or see with the ear. The nose, tongue, and body exercise power over making the support beautiful, protecting the body, producing consciousness with its concordant factors, and the unique <unclear>...</unclear> of tasting flavors and touching tangibles. If those are impaired, one is not beautiful. By enjoying physical food, one protects the body; the others are the same. The male, female, life, and mind faculties each exercise power over two purposes. For a moment, the male and female faculties exercise power over the divisions and distinctions of sentient beings. At the beginning of this eon <term>kalpa</term> of the first perfection, before the male and female faculties had arisen, there were no such distinctions. Once the male and female faculties arose, the distinctions of male and female names, shapes, and voices <note>original: ro "taste/flavor", likely meaning "tone" here</note> also arose. Some assert that those faculties also exercise power over thorough affliction and complete purification. For the four—eunuchs who lack those faculties and hermaphrodites whose faculties are impaired, the envious etc.—do not have non-vows, the immediate <term>anantarya</term> sins, or the cutting of roots of virtue. They also do not have vows, the attainment of the fruits <note>of the path</note>, or the abandonment of passions. Those endowed with male or female faculties do possess those earlier and later sets of qualities. The life faculty exercises power over two: the linking of the concordant class and the perfect maintenance. At the conclusion of a life-existence, when linking to the birth-existence of the intermediate state <term>bardo</term> without a support, one obtains life and thus its power is established there. After that, until that existence is shifted, it perfectly maintains and causes one to stay, thus its power is established.

<leaf-break/>

...based on the object, from mental happiness, the yearning for renunciation is born. Likewise, from mental consciousness based on phenomena, through mental happiness, up to the birth of the yearning for renunciation, mental unhappiness and equanimity are also included and relied upon; therefore, it is asserted that the three—mental happiness, unhappiness, and equanimity—also exercise power over the types of purification. Here, the Sautrantikas, illustrating with examples, say: It is not tenable for the Vaibhashikas to assert that the eye and ear protect the body. For by merely seeing a thief with the eye or hearing the thief's <unclear>...</unclear> with the ear, one cannot protect the body. It is the mental consciousness, together with its concordant factors, that knows that danger and causes one to avoid it. The assertion that the faculties exercise power over making the body beautiful is also untenable. The support of the faculty <note>the physical organ</note> makes it beautiful, but the faculties themselves transcend the objects of the faculties, so it is not established that they make it beautiful. Therefore, according to the Vaibhashika view, only the power of the five faculties to produce consciousness together with concordant factors is tenable; the other claims are rejected—this is the Sautrantika system. Second, the Sautrantika scripture: "Over their own objects and over all, because they exercise power in perceiving, they are faculties." ...will become equal. "From the body, the first <note>female</note> and second <note>male</note> faculties..." because they exercise power over the concordant, the thoroughly afflicted, and the types of purification. "Life and feelings, and likewise faith, were previously asserted to be faculties. Because they exercise power over obtaining whatever nirvana from wherever, the faculty of making known all that is not known, the faculty of knowing all, and likewise the faculty of being endowed with knowing all." Thus, if the word "mostly" indicates that those assertions of the Vaibhashikas are untenable, then how is your own assertion? Among those faculties from the eye to the mind, the five like the eye and body exercise power over perceiving their respective five objects; for without those five faculties, there would be no unrestrained perception of the objects. For a person, they are the causes for the continuation of perceiving objects. The mind faculty exercises power over perceiving all objects from the perceived up to phenomena, because the mind faculty causes one to enter into the perception of all objects. Here, if one argues that the objects should also exercise power over perception because without objects and meanings, there would be no perception, it does not pervade. Because one does not know the perceiver of the distinct objects, and the distinct objects are not the cause of the general stream of consciousness. Following the clarity or lack of clarity, the eye etc. do not act as the controllers. The first is established: because it enters into power, by the distinct objects <unclear>...</unclear> the eye faculty cannot act as the general cause for the arising of eye consciousness perceiving its object. The second is established: by helping or harming the object, there is no help or harm to the eye faculty.

<leaf-break/>

Then, the life faculty exercises power over staying in the concordant class, but food does not. The second point is established: the feeling faculties starting with pleasure exercise power primarily over thorough affliction, because through the gate of perceiving and being concordant with pleasure, the affliction of desire is produced; this was spoken by the <unclear>...</unclear>. Therefore, the assertion of some Vaibhashikas that even the pleasure faculty exercises power over purification is refuted. Although they may enter as mere conditions for purification, they are not the actual causes that exercise primary power. Regarding the five—faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—each is a faculty because they all exercise power over the process of complete purification. This is established: mindfulness and the other four, at the stage of "heat" on the path of preparation, suppress the afflictions that are obstacles to the birth of the path through faith and so forth. At the stage of "supreme dharma" on the path of preparation, since there is no cause for a balanced share <note>equanimity</note>, the power of faith and so forth also leads one to the path that transcends the world. Therefore, because "purification" here refers to entering the path, they exercise power over the stages and paths of faith and so forth. Regarding the faculty of making known, since it is not the path of transcending, it is not called "exercising power" there. The faculty of making known all that is not known, the faculty of knowing all, and the faculty of being endowed with knowing all are faculties because they exercise power progressively higher over the manifestation of the aggregates of nirvana and so forth. This is established: because the faculty of making known the nirvana is the path of seeing, it exercises power over the path of meditation that knows all. That in turn exercises power over the path of learning <term>shaiksha</term> for one endowed with knowing all. That in turn has no power over the final nirvana. # Om Svasti! Homage to the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
This is "Meaningful to Behold," the manual for the instruction of the Profound Path of Vajra Yoga, the single path traveled by all the Conquerors and their Sons.
Homage to the Guru and the glorious Vajrasattva!
Homage to the unchanging bliss and the wisdom of the union of Mahamudra!
I pay homage to the holy ones who are perfectly bound by the nectar of supreme accomplishment!
The foundation of all excellence, the Guru's state is like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
To the one who strives for all beings, I bow with devotion at the Guru's feet.
The all-pervading expanse is of all forms; mind itself is the treasury of all natural qualities.
Inseparable and primordially liberated Dharmakaya; may the unchanging ultimate self-awareness flourish!
Whatever has emerged from the great ocean of the mind through a hundred thousand rivers of Tantric classes,
From that, may the stream of instructions contained in the vase of the heart bring good fortune to this region.
Herein is the unsurpassed essence of all the Sutras and Tantras, the source of all mundane and trans-mundane attainments, the ultimate supreme path traveled by all Buddhas of the three times, the gateway for all lords of yogis without exception. To the Vajra body endowed with the six elements, one should act as follows:
The instruction on Refuge, the root of general Dharma; the instruction on the Generation of Bodhicitta, the root of the Great Vehicle; the instruction on the Hundred Syllables, which purifies sins and obscurations; the instruction on the Mandala, which gathers the accumulations; and the instruction on Guru Yoga, the root of blessings—these are the five.
First: In a solitary place, sit on a comfortable seat in a posture that roughly accords with the key points of the body. Having settled the mind, imagine that this very region where you are residing becomes a great, vast, and wide pure land. In its center is a celestial palace made of various jewels, without limit in size or dimension. In its center is a wish-fulfilling tree with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit in full bloom. On its crown, on a high and wide throne of various jewels supported by lions, upon seats of stacked lotuses, suns, and moons, is the Root Guru in the form of Vajradhara, surrounded by all the lineage gurus, the assembly of deities of the Yidam Conquerors, and the hosts of guardians of the teachings, the Dakinis and Dharma Protectors who possess the eye of wisdom. They reside there in the manner of teachers. On the four sides of the wish-fulfilling tree, on the ground inside the palace, clearly visualize high and wide seats of lion-thrones, lotuses, suns, and moons. In front of the Guru's body...
<leaf-break/>
...reciting thus, remember the qualities of the Guru and the Three Jewels, and having placed your trust entirely in the Three Jewels through fear of the sufferings of samsara, perform the refuge as much as you can.
When ending the session, pray three times: "I pray that the Guru and the Precious Jewels grant blessings to me and all sentient beings!" The objects of refuge melt into light and dissolve into yourself. Perform the dedication of the virtue of taking refuge: "By this virtue, may all people complete the accumulations of merit and wisdom, and may they obtain the two holy bodies <note>Rupakaya and Dharmakaya</note> that arise from merit and wisdom." Recite such appropriate verses.
The first cycle of visualization, the instruction on Refuge, is finished. After the visualization has been explained in this way, have the students maintain the visualization of taking refuge for two or three days or as appropriate. Furthermore, if the student is eager to listen and the Guru is eager to explain, the student will be suitable to understand. If the important necessary meanings are explained, they will understand and their minds will turn toward the Dharma. If it is mere talk, the mind will not turn toward the Dharma as before. If it is a type that must be explained with certainty, then while the students are maintaining the visualization, explain the core meaning of refuge in the Sutras and Mantras or the Great and Small Vehicles daily, so that it definitely integrates with their minds.

Then, place a black stone, a clod of earth, or some object that does not harm the eyes and is not too large in front of yourself. From the path of the gaze, gradually lower the empty-form onto that object. While still seeing that object, strain the mind into the empty-form and meditate. By meditating like that, if you see both the empty-form and the object of karmic appearance equally, it is the inferior way of appearing; although there is not much enhancement, if you familiarize yourself for a long time, it will reach the vital point. For some, immediately the object of karmic appearance is not seen, and only the sign of Clear Light is seen. This seems like a very good way of appearing, but it is the middling way, so no great increase will come. Again, if both the sign-appearance and the karmic-appearance vanish at once, and for a while nothing at all appears, it is quick—

<leaf-break/>

This is the twelfth cycle of visualization. Second: it is mostly the same as during the branch of Withdrawal, except that when sleeping, one directs the mind to the empty-form itself. By going to sleep without being interrupted by discursive thoughts, the Clear Light of sleep will be quickly caught. If you are able to make the empty-form appear inside your own body, then draw the empty-form into the heart. If you go to sleep while directing the mind to that, there is no doubt that the Clear Light of sleep will be caught at that very moment. This is the thirteenth cycle of visualization. Second, the establishing of the meaning of meditation in the mind: the definition of Meditation <term>dhyana</term>, the timing of meditation, the branches of the way of meditating, the measure of the signs of meditation, the divisions of the objects to be purified and the purifiers, and the result obtained by meditating. Among these six, first: *dhyana* means the mind is without movement regarding the object of visualization. Just as when a door-bolt is well inserted, the door-panels do not wobble and one gains mastery over opening and closing the door, it means gaining power over the object of visualization. From the *Stainless Light*: "The ten objects and subjects are meditated upon as manifold forms in a single state." Thus, one makes the mind one-pointed upon the Clear Light of the empty-forms possessed of all supreme aspects, and gains the power to remain or move as one wishes.

<leaf-break/>

Regarding the inner visualization, Samadhi <gloss>Meditative Absorption</gloss> itself is the experience of it arising as bliss; it is the branch of unwavering bliss. Using that as a condition, the body being pervaded by a special, highly processed bliss is the further benefit of unwavering bliss. Furthermore, first, Wisdom alone is born. Then it occurs together with Conception. Likewise, it occurs together with three: Discernment; together with four: Joy; and together with five: Unwavering Bliss. At that time, the branch of Meditation is perfected and born in the continuum. If one maintains that continuously and meditates, the qualities of culmination will quickly be born. Fourth: from the Tantra: "In the center of that, the Buddha-form is the Sambhogakaya, manifold and free from objects and aspects." This shows the uncommon signs of Meditation. The reflections of all the three worlds subsumed in the ten signs are seen much more intensely than during the previous Withdrawal. The manifold reflections of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, which are also of various colors, are seen marked by many drops <term>tilaka</term> possessing the five qualities: radiating light, being subtle, shimmering, vibrating, and being difficult to destroy. In the center of the drops, many Buddha-reflections appear. Furthermore, by realizing them as the appearances of the mind itself being pure, all the karmic appearances of the relative truth appear naturally as like illusions. From the *Later Tantra*—

...and make a private room. In the southwest, the direction of the <term>Rākṣasa</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, make a retreat house and a protector temple. In the northwest, the direction of the Wind God, place the prayer wheels, hail protection, and the storehouse for robes and cushions. In the north, partition a large area to make an offering hall. Place the two doors for the northeast and northwest within that. Below that offering hall, establish a house for the <term>Yakṣas</term> <gloss>wealth spirits</gloss> and make a hidden treasury. In the western wing of the great hall, make a grain storehouse. Below that, designate a Naga house and a stable for livestock. Use the eastern veranda for empowerments, Dharma teachings, and so forth. On the south side, make a kitchen and a general storehouse. In the center, keep the upper and lower levels open to each other. On the side walls, use <unclear>...</unclear> beams, stacked wood, and top-carvings; it should be made like a divine palace of great distinction. Its qualities are: in the short term, it inspires clarity and virtuous practice naturally increases. By offering it while visualizing it as a divine celestial mansion, the Jewels are pleased and the accumulation of merit is perfected. The Ḍākinīs and Dharma Protectors are pleased, activities are accomplished, and wealth gathers. By captivating the minds of those to be tamed, it will become a place of worship for all. Avoid placements that cause enmity; let the private mill rotate in the depths of the inner courtyard. Do not have the dragon roar at the doorstep. Do not place the southern pantry and northern mill [incorrectly]. Aim the steep slope toward the depths and...

<leaf-break/>

From the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, or eleventh [day], take various grains from a wealthy and fortunate person and place them in a vase. Also, take five kinds of silk, five kinds of medicine, five kinds of grain, five kinds of precious gems, and cloth that has not been worn by a widow. Fill it with breast milk from a mother whose parents, son, and husband are all alive, milk from white and yellow cows, and milk from a white goat. Fill it with the three whites and three sweets. On a day with good planets and stars during the waxing moon of any of the four seasonal months, arrange offerings to the Jewels. Place the vase on a heap of rice. Four monks should invite the Naga King Varuṇa from the southern ocean according to the ritual of the eight Nagas. Within the vase, which has become the great palace of the Nagas, summon the sons and retinue with their wealth three times and dissolve them into it. Recite the "Heart of Dependent Origination" and auspicious verses, and place it in a hollow in the wall at least one cubit high in the center of the house. Offer incense and the three whites, and make prayers for desired goals. Plaster it over and draw the sun, moon, and an auspicious stupa. By this, wealth and enjoyments will increase, and whether for the Sangha, a king, or a yogi, the teachings will flourish and spread.
Again, at the end of time, when border armies such as the <term>Turukha</term> <gloss>Turks/invaders</gloss> or other foreign kings and their troops attack repeatedly for years, months, or days...

<leaf-break/>

The oral instruction: take earth from a wrathful place such as the Black Stupa of Samye and mix it with black soil. Make an image of the enemy. In the heart, place a six-spoked wheel on poison-paper. In the center, write the names of whatever border armies or enemies you wish to guard against, visualizing them dissolving there. Write: "May all their movements and evil intentions be <term>JAMBHAYA NANA</term> <gloss>crushed</gloss>, <term>MOHAYA NANA</term> <gloss>bewildered</gloss>, <term>OṂ LAṂ HŪṂ LAṂ STAMBHAYA</term> <gloss>paralyzed</gloss>, <term>RAKṢUMARA YANA NANA</term>." Around the outer circle, write: "May the bodies of the great moving border armies, the hostile enemy troops, harming obstacles, bad harvests, plagues, times of strife, and all great terrors be <term>STAMBHAYA NANA</term> <gloss>paralyzed</gloss>." Smear the <term>liṅga</term> <gloss>effigy</gloss> with poison and blood. Pierce the four limbs with the "Ja" spikes. Use the mantra of a Yidam deity in which you have completed the approach and accomplishment and possess power. For the former enemies, later enemies, or whichever enemy is targeted, perform the suppression forcefully and dissolve them. Then, in the aforementioned direction, a cubit deep, make a good stone box. Place the <term>liṅga</term> inside the heart of a clay fish. Drive a ritual dagger <term>kīla</term> into it. Place skulls facing outward on top. Press it down with a stupa made of whatever material is available. If a large stupa is built, the aforementioned items can be placed inside the "Mount Meru" <note>the central pillar</note> of the stupa. Then, prepare four ritual cakes <term>tormas</term>. At each stupa, enthrone the Four Kings, invite them, and perform praises and entrustment of activities in a great accomplishment ceremony...

ཉོན་མོངས་དབང་བྱས་སྨྱོན་པ་ལྟ་བུའི་སེཾས་། ལོག་པར་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་ངན་དུ་ལེ་དུ་ཞུཌ་། མགོན་མེད་སྐྱབས་བྲལ་གཅིག་པུར་རྣཾ་པར་འཁྱཾས་། རྐྱེན་དང་མི་ལྡན་སྡིག་པའི་གྲོཌ་ཀྱིས་
ཟིན་། དེ་ལྟར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་ད་རུང་མི་སྐྱོ་བར་། སྡུག་བསྔལ་མ་ཤེས་ཀུན་འབྱུང་རྒྱན་དུ་མཐོང་། དལ་འབྱོར་འཛོམ་ཡང་ཐར་པའི་བློ་མེད་པར་། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལ་ཆཌ་པའི་
གཏི་མུག་ཅན་། མཐའ་མེད་འཁོར་བར་ཉི་ཐག་ཚུལ་འདི་ལ་། བརྩེ་ལྡན་སེཾས་དཔའ་རྣཾས་ཀྱིས་ལ་བཟོད་། སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་ཡང་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཞིང་། ཐབས་
དང་ཤེས་རབ་དབྱེར་མེད་གཟིངས་བཏང་ནས་། དེད་དཔོན་མཁས་པའི་མཉན་པར་ལྡན་པ་ཡིས་། སྲིད་པའི་མཚོ་ལས་ངེས་པར་བསྒྲལ་ནས་ནི་། ཐར་པའི་སྐམས་སར་
སླར་དུ་གདོན་བྱ་ཞིང་། བདག་བདེ་དམན་པའི་བསཾ་པ་བོར་ནས་ནི་། རྒྱུན་ཆད་མེད་པའི་གཞན་དོན་འབད་པར་བྱ་། དེང་སང་དུས་ན་ཆོས་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་རྣཾས་ས་
བསྟན་པའི་སྲོག་དང་སྙིང་པོར་གྱུར་པ་ཡི་། ཟློག་དང་བསྟཾན་ཡལ་བར་དོར་ནས་ནི་། རང་དགར་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་ཁ་ཟས་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་། རབ་བྱུང་རྣཾས་ཀྱང་བསྟན་པའི་རྩ་བ་
<leaf-break/>
࿓࿔་། པའི་བསྟན་པ་དྲི་མེད་ཉཾས་དགའ་འདི་། ལྐོག་མར་དབུཌ་འབྱིན་འདྲ་བར་གྱུར་འདི་ལ་། ནུས་པ་མེད་ཀྱང་སེཾས་ཀྱིས་ག་ལ་བཟོད་། བློ་གྲོས་ལྡན་པས་སྙིང་སྟོབས་
བསྐྱེད་བྱ་སྟེ་། བག་ཡོད་མཆོག་གི་བརྟུལ་ཞུཌ་གཟུང་ནས་ཀྱང་། བསྟན་པ་གནས་དང་རྒྱས་པའི་ཐབས་འབད་ཅིང་། ཕྱོཌ་རྣཾས་ཀུན་ཏུ་བསྲུང་ཞིང་སྤེལ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པ་ཚར་བཅད་
དམ་པ་མཆོད་བྱ་ཞིང་། ཀུན་ནས་ཀུན་ཏུ་བསྟན་ལ་གང་ཕན་བྱ་། འདི་བཀོད་དགེ་བས་མཁའ་མཉཾ་འགྲོ་བ་ཀུན་། ངན་འགྲོའི་ལཾ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་རྒྱུན་བཅད་ནས་། ཟབ་དང་
རྒྱ་ཆེའི་ཆོས་ལ་བརྩོན་བྱས་ཏེ་། དོན་གཉིས་མཐར་ཕྱིན་སྐུ་གསུཾ་མྱུར་རྒྱས་ཤོག་། བདག་ཉིད་རྟག་ཏུ་སྤྲུལ་པའི་གཟུཌ་འཛིན་ཅིང་། སདྱས་བསྟན་པ་ཕྱོཌ་བཅུར་སྒྲོགས་པ་དང་།
རིནེ་བླ་མའི་ཐུཌ་དགོངས་རྫོཌ་བྱེད་ཅིང་། འཕྲིས་སྣ་ཚོཌ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་གཡོག་པོར་ཤོག་། འགྲོ་དོན་གྱི་ལག་ལེན་སེང་གེའི་འབྲུག་སྒྲ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་། སློབ་དཔོན་བསོད་ནཾས་བྱང་ཆུབ་
རྒྱལ་མཚན་གྱི་གསུང་མ་བཅག་པར་། ཤཱཀྱའི་དགེ་སློང་ཡང་དགོན་བས་དཔལ་གྱི་རིའི་ལྷོ་ཕྱོཌ་སུ་བཀོད་པ་ཨྠིི་། །།ན་མོ་རཏྣ་གུ་རུ་། སྐྱབས་མེད་སྐྱོབ་

࿓࿔་། འཁོར་བའི་དངོས་གཞི་ལ་། རྟོཌ་ན་མྱང་འདས་དངོས་གཞི་རུ་། ཇི་ལྟར་མ་བཅོས་རང་ཉིད་དེ་། རང་བཞིན་ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་ཞེས་བརྗོད་། ལུས་
ངག་ཡིད་གསུཾ་དབྱེར་མེད་གཤིས་། སྐུ་གསུཾ་ངོ་བོ་ཡེ་གནས་ལ་། བླ་མེད་སྔཌ་ཀྱི་ཁྱདར་རོ་། འཁྲུལ་པ་ལྡོག་དང་རང་མཚན་ཉིད་། རྟོཌ་གོཾས་མཐར་ཕྱིན་མངོན་བྱེད་

ཟུང་འཇུག་སྟེ་། ལཾ་ཤེས་ལཾ་གྱི་མཆོག་ཡིནོ་། གང་དང་གང་སྣང་དེ་ཉིད་ཡིན་། དེ་ལ་རྣཾ་པར་དཀར་བའི་ཆོས་། ཚང་ཞིང་མ་ནོར་ཕུན་ཚོཌ་པས་། ཅི་བྱས་རྣམ་

All mother beings, pervasive as space, covered by immeasurable kindness, are submerged in this ocean of existence through ignorance. They turn their backs on the path of liberation. Their minds, like madmen under the power of afflictions, act perversely and enter into evil ways. Without a protector or refuge, they wander alone. They are seized by sinful friends and lack the right conditions. Even so, they are not yet weary; not knowing suffering, they see its origin as an ornament. Even if they possess the freedoms and fortunes, they lack the mind of liberation and are ignorant, attached to perversions. Toward this state of being like a sunbeam in endless samsara, how can compassionate Bodhisattvas endure it? Without abandoning them for even a moment, they launch the boat of inseparable method and wisdom. With the skillful captain's rowing, they will certainly cross the ocean of existence and be brought again to the dry land of liberation. Casting aside the thought of one's own lowly happiness, one should strive continuously for the benefit of others. Nowadays, those who have entered the Dharma have abandoned the reversals and the essence which is the life-force of the teaching. Acting as they please, they pursue only food. Even the ordained, who are the root of the teaching...

This stainless and delightful teaching of the Buddha has become like a breath caught in the throat. Even if one lacks power, how can the mind endure this? One possessed of intelligence should generate courage and, having taken up the supreme asceticism of heedfulness, strive in methods for the teaching to remain and flourish. Protect and spread it in all directions, subdue the perverse, honor the holy, and do whatever is helpful for the teaching in every way. By the virtue of composing this, may all beings as pervasive as space cut the stream of the path and results of the lower realms. Having exerted themselves in the profound and extensive Dharma, may they perfect the two benefits <note>for self and others</note> and quickly flourish in the Three Bodies. May I myself always hold an emanation body, proclaim the Buddha's teaching in the ten directions, fulfill the intentions of the precious Gurus, and be a servant who accomplishes various enlightened activities. This work called "The Lion's Thunder: The Practice of Benefiting Beings," written without altering the words of Master Sonam Changchub Gyaltsen, was composed by the Shakya monk Yanggonpa in the southern part of the Glorious Mountain. *Asthi.* Homage to the Jewel Guru. The protector of the unprotected, the supreme refuge, the glory is the Lord of Dharma, the Protector of Beings. To the one with the eye of all-seeing wisdom, the holder of the Vajra, I bow at your lotus feet. Regarding the three—Ground, Path, and Fruit...

...in the core of samsara. If realized, it is the core of nirvana; just as it is, unfabricated, it is called the "Co-emergent Nature." The nature of the inseparability of body, speech, and mind is the Three Bodies eternally present—this is the distinction of the Unsurpassed Secret Mantra. Because it reverses delusion and makes the perfection of the realization and training of its own characteristics manifest, it is called the "Unmistaken Certain Path." That path is method and wisdom—emptiness and compassion. It is the perfection of the two truths, the two stages, and the two collections. The two are the non-dual union—knowing the path is the supreme path. Whatever appears is just that. Because the Dharmas of the white side <note>virtue</note> are complete, mistaken-free, and perfect, whatever is done is the path of omniscience. From this, Buddhahood is not far. The support for practice is the possession of the characteristics of freedoms and fortunes. Those of the lineage of practice possess sharp faculties; in the end, they have faith and perfect diligence. The wisdom that knows that meaning is possessed. The outer dominant condition is the supreme Spiritual Friend. The inner dominant condition is the method of accumulation and purification. The core path is the self-liberation of causes and conditions. The objective condition is the pure, unmistaken view. The immediate condition is the path of the lower stages; the power of training in the higher stages arises naturally. If it is absent, the mind of enlightenment does not arise. ན་དངོ་གྲུབ་ཡིན་། མོས་གུས་བྱེད་པ་གནད་དུ་ཐོང་། ཚེ་འདིའི་སྐྱིད་སྡུག་རྨི་ལཾ་ཡིན་། ཅིས་ཀྱང་དགོས་མེད་བློ་སྣ་བསྟུངས་། བདེན་མེད་སྣང་བ་ཟོག་མ་ཡིན་། ཆཌ་
མེད་སྒྱུ་མའི་ཟོལ་འགྲོཌ་གྱིས་། འགྲོ་དོན་གཙོ་བོ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་། རྣལྱོར་གཙོ་བོ་གསུཾ་ཁོང་དུ་སྦྱོངས་། བྱེད་མཁན་ཐཾད་རིག་པ་ཡིན་། རང་སྣང་འགྲོ་ལྡོག་གཏན་
<leaf-break/>
༄༅།
།༄༅། །དྲན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། བདག་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་བདག་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། དྲན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་

...an ornament of the four continents. The holy attendant, who possesses the seven precious possessions of exceptional wealth, is also his glory. His intelligence is sharp-spoked and its hub is service to the teachings. Because he is skilled in the methods of the four ways of gathering, whatever millions of wealth and followers he controls are the precious wheel of vast activities. Through the giving of one who is skilled in generosity, who has many objects of giving and a spacious internal capacity despite showing little, and who protects the lowly while holding the high—the hearts of those with desires find the fulfillment of their wishes; he is the precious wish-fulfilling jewel. He has the speech of a holy person, pleasant to the ear, and his beautiful conduct is sought by all and virtuous. Through the fragrance of his wisdom, learning, and mindfulness, he makes the mind very joyful; he is the precious woman. From the great treasury of vast and skillful practice, protection, and increase, his great conduct is not impoverished and his use is not exhausted; he binds the great, gathers the small, and does not leave out those in great need. He is the precious householder, the foundation of wealth. He is not disturbed by much criticism and does not shrink from great poverty. Lord of the copper mountains who is unmoved by the conduct of the unruly, whose Mahayana capacity is vast, relaxed, and without limits, and who can accommodate all good and bad—he is the precious elephant. In the supreme form of mindfulness, awareness, and discipline...

<leaf-break/>

...all are held by the three precious ones. Just as a good bed makes the body and mind comfortable, when visitors from all directions arrive without anything, he welcomes them with smiles and pleasantries at whatever time they arrive. He is the fourth precious thing, satisfying the close friends and protectors. Just as poison and iron-poison <note>or "poison-remedy"</note> pacify the levels of heat, he is warm-hearted within and open-handed without. In seeking, hiding, and receiving pleasant things and so forth, he does not waste or lose but protects all; he is the fifth precious thing. Just as fine clothes make the body and mind happy when touched, in the place, the vessel, and all objects of use, he is clean, prepared, and free from the stain of filth; he is the sixth precious thing, pleasing the heart of whoever sees. Just as the supreme sword achieves its purpose when brandished, through his harmonious conduct toward those near and far without distinction, he captures the hearts of all and is loving toward all; he is the seventh precious thing, accomplishing all activities. The supreme attendant possesses these seven precious qualities, and the sub-attendants have their own seven precious things. Here on this earth, those with the gods are delighted; let them be established in joy and devotion! In the treasury where the purposes of both are accomplished, the excellent vase of love is filled with the superior water. The crown-ornament of faith and the mind of devotion are beautiful; the tongue of intelligence is agile and free from the stain of self-interest. This is the wondrous treasury...

<leaf-break/>

...the precious source of all needs and desires. In the non-conceptual space of the ultimate, the deceptive results of the relative appear as dependent origination. The needs of both self and others are accomplished. If one has devotion, blessings arise. If one prays, realization dawns. If one leaves a karmic connection, one becomes a disciple to be tamed. I bow at the feet of the qualified Guru, whose seeing, hearing, and touching are meaningful. To the faithful who fear birth and death: please make practice your essence by letting go of activities through renunciation! Since the instructions exist, keep them in your mind. The phenomena of cyclic existence have no true existence. Generate weariness and let go of activities! The life-force is impermanent and death follows. Practice the Dharma with "dry meat" urgency! To the Guru, who is the Buddha of the three times, purify your perception and pray! When many appearances of circumstances arise, they are blessings. Do not accept or reject; take them as the path. Skillful means arise in whatever way he acts. Do not look at faults; abandon wrong perceptions! If your heart and mind merge, that is the accomplishment <term>siddhi</term>. Take the practice of devotion as the vital point! The happiness and suffering of this life are a dream. Shorten your mental activities regarding unnecessary things! Non-existent appearances are not deceptive. Act with the unattached manner of an illusion! The primary purpose of beings is practice. Train in the three primary yogas! The one who acts is awareness itself. Constantly...

<leaf-break/>

Possessing mindfulness, and possessing a self, and possessing mindfulness, and possessing a self, and possessing mindfulness, and possessing a self, and mindfulness, and mindfulness, and a self, and mindfulness by mindfulness, and mindfulness by mindfulness by mindfulness, and mindfulness, and mindfulness by self, and mindfulness with, and mindfulness as mindfulness self, and mindfulness to self mindfulness, and mindfulness in self, and mindfulness others, and mindful by mindfulness, mindfulness by mindfulness by self...

࿓࿔་། བྱུང་དོགས་འདུག་ན་། སྙིང་མེད་ཚེ་ཁ་ནང་དུ་ལོག་མ་བསཾ་མནོ་ཟོངས་དང་། འཁོར་བ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་མེ་དོང་ན་། འགྲོ་དྲུག་ལས་
ངན་གྱི་རླུང་གིས་བདས་ནས་། ཀུན་འབྱུང་སྲིད་པའི་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་ལ་། བདེ་སྐྱིད་ཀྱི་གོ་སྐབས་འདུག་གཾ་སོམས་དང་། ངན་སོང་མི་ཁོམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་གནས་ནས་།
དུས་ལན་ཅིག་དལ་འབྱོར་རིནོེ་། འཛོམ་དཀའི་རྟཻལ་འཛོམ་དུས་སུ་། ཆོས་མིན་གྱི་བྱ་ལོང་འདུག་གཾ་སོམས་དང་།ད་འདི་ནས་ཐར་ལཾ་གྱི་རྡོག་སྣ་འགྲེད་
ན་། དུས་གཏིང་མཐའ་མེད་པའི་སྡུག་འབོད་ཞིག་འཛུཌ་པས་། ཚེ་འདི་ཀུན་གྱི་སྐྱིད་སྡུག་རྫུན་པོ་ཡིནོ་། གནས་ངན་སོང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཨེ་
བཟོད་སོམས་དང་། ཚེ་མི་རྟག་འཆི་བས་གཏིང་ནས་ཐུག་། ཤོམ་ར་དལ་འབྱོར་གྱི་ཚེ་ཞབས་ཟད་། བསྡད་དུ་རེའི་ལོང་ལ་ཡིད་ལ་མེད་ཅིག་ཡོང་
ན་། ཆོས་བྱའོ་སྙཾ་པའི་ཡིད་སྨོན་གྱིས་ཕན་ནམ་སོམས་དང་། རང་ཟད་ཀ་ནས་སྐྱེས་པའི་མི་ཆོས་བཤིག་། ཕ་ཡུལ་དང་གཉེན་འབྲེལ་རྒྱབ་
ཏུ་བསྒྱུར་། དད་སྐྱེས་ཆོས་སྒོར་ཁྱུང་པ་མིན་ནམ་། ལྡམ་ལྡོམ་ལ་བསྡད་དུ་ཁོམ་མམ་སོམས་དང་། ཚེ་འདིའི་ཚེ་ཐབས་སྒྲུབ་པ་བས་ཀྱང་།
<leaf-break/>
࿓࿔་། པ་ཡང་མེད་པར་། ད་ངན་སོང་དུ་ལོག་ན་ཕམ་ཚབས་ཆེའོ་། མི་སྙིང་ཅན་ཀུན་རང་ལ་ཕྱི་ཐག་སྲིངས་ལ་། རང་མི་བསླུ་ན་འཆི་ཆོས་
ཞེ་ནས་རེ་མཛོད་དང་། ལྟེམ་རྐྱང་མེད་པའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བསྐུལ་ལ་། རྒྱུན་ཆད་མེད་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ་མཛོད་ལ་། དུས་ད་རེས་འཁོར་བ་དང་གཏན་གྱིས་
མཛོད་ཅིག་། དབྱངས་དེ་ཀུན་བསཾ་མནོ་དགུ་ཡི་དབྱངས་། ར་སྔོན་ན་བཞུཌ་པའི་སྒོམ་ཆེན་ལ་། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་བཞེངས་བསྐུལ་བཏབ་པ་ཡིན་། རང་
མེད་ཀྱི་གཞན་བསྐུལ་མི་རིཌ་ཏེ་། སྨྲ་འདོད་ཀྱི་ཁ་ལ་གསོལ་མ་ཐེབས་། ཁྱེད་མད་སྙཾ་གྱི་བདེན་ཤེས་མ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་རུ་སྒོམས་ལ་གསན་པ་
ཞུ་། བསཾ་མནོ་དགུ་པ་ཨྠིི་། ་།སྐུ་རྡོེ་སྐྱིལ་ཀྲུང་ལ་བཞུཌ་པའི་དུས་སུ་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་གྱི་རྟོཌ་པ་རོ་གཅིག་ཏུ་འཕྲོད་ནས་། ནུས་ཅིག་ཅིར་སྣང་
ཐཾད་རང་སར་གྲོལ་བ་ཞིག་བྱུང་ནས་། ལྟ་སྒོམ་སྤྱོད་འབྲས་སྟོར་བའི་སྒོམ་ཆ་ལང་མའི་མགུར་འདི་བཞེསོ་། རྡོེ་འཆང་ཆེན་ཡི་གཟུཌ་ཅན་། དོན་རང་
ལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཡཻས་དེ་། ལག་པའི་མཐིལ་དུ་གཏེར་ཅིག་སྤྲད་ནས་། སྤང་བྱ་རང་གྲོལ་གྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སོ་། འཁོར་འདས་བསྲེ་བའི་རྩལ་པོ་
<leaf-break/>
࿓࿔་། ཉིན་མཚན་དགེ་བས་དུས་འདའ་ཞིང་། ཅི་བྱེད་སེཾས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་སྦྱོར་། བཟང་ངན་གྱི་རྐྱེན་ལ་རོ་སྙོཾས་བྱེད་། ཅི་འདྲའི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཞིག་

ཀྱིས་། མཐར་ཕྱིན་སྐུཾ་གསུཾ་གྱི་སདྱས་འགྲུས་། ཅི་འདྲའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་ལས་། དེ་རིང་སྤྲང་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་སྟོར་། འབྲས་བུ་དེ་བསྒྲུབ་བྱ་མེད་དུ་

If you are afraid of what might happen, think in your heart: is there any chance for happiness and bliss in the cause and effect of existence, driven by the winds of bad karma of the six types of beings in the fire-pit of the suffering of <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>? During this time when the precious freedoms and advantages, so difficult to find, are assembled for once from the rebirths of the lower realms and the restless states, think: is there time for activities that are not the Dharma? If you slip at the threshold of the path to liberation now, you will establish a cry of suffering that has no end in the depths. Therefore, the happiness and suffering of all this life is a lie. Think: can you endure the suffering of the lower realms? Life is impermanent and will finally meet with death. The time of freedom and advantage is being exhausted. If a time comes that you did not expect, think: will the wishful thinking of wanting to do Dharma help then? Break the worldly ways born from your own exhaustion. Turn your back on your homeland and relatives. Are you not one who has dived into the door of Dharma through born faith? Think: is there leisure to remain in a state of indifference? More than achieving the means of this life—
<leaf-break/>
Without even that, if you return to the lower realms now, the loss will be great. All people of heart, extend your long-term perspective. If you would not deceive yourself, place your hopes in the Dharma of death from your heart. Spurred by diligent effort without hesitation, perform continuous practice. At this time, settle the matter with <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss> once and for all. All these melodies are the melodies of the nine reflections. I have issued an urging to diligence for the great meditator residing in the blue place. It is not right to urge others when I have nothing myself, but I could not stop my mouth from wanting to speak. Even if the realization of truth has not been born, thinking "You are right," please listen with compassion. This is the Ninth Reflection. When sitting in the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>diamond</gloss> cross-legged posture, having met with the single taste of the realization free from elaboration, a power arose where whatever appears is liberated in its own place. Then, he sang this song of the vibrant meditation that loses the distinctions of view, meditation, conduct, and fruit. The Great <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra Holder</gloss> in visible form gave a treasure of the wisdom that exists within oneself into the palm of the hand; he is skillful in the means of self-liberation of that which is to be abandoned. The great power of mixing <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss> and <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>transcendence of suffering</gloss>—
<leaf-break/>
Spending the time in virtue day and night, whatever is done is applied to the benefit of sentient beings. Treating the conditions of good and bad with equal taste, such a conduct existed, but today the conduct of the beggar is lost. That conduct has vanished without a trace of value. Through the way the four yogas of meditation arise, and the signs of warmth of the five paths and ten stages, the Buddha of the three bodies is perfected at the end. Such a fruit existed, but today the fruit of the beggar is lost. That fruit has vanished into a state where there is nothing to be achieved. In the natural state where the Three Jewels are self-perfected, even prostrations and offerings were not found. Making the Lama and one's own mind inseparable, the act of praying was not found. In the self-arisen three bodies of the six types of beings, the meditation on compassion was not found. Since there is no <term>Yidam</term> <gloss>meditational deity</gloss> other than oneself, the requesting of accomplishments was not found. In the equality where the dependence of self and other is exhausted, a place to perform the benefit of others was not found. Within the sphere of meditating on appearance and awareness, a spontaneous cessation was not found. Whatever is done is solely virtue, so something non-virtuous to be guarded against was not found. Whatever arises is vibrantly clear in the luminosity—

ཆེན་བླ་མ་ལ་། དབྱེར་མེད་དུས་འདིའི་མོས་གུས་བགྱིད་། སྤྲང་པོ་རི་ཁྲོད་རས་པ་ལ་། མཚན་ལྡན་བླ་མའི་བཀའ་དྲིན་གྱིས་། རྟོཌ་པ་རྡོ་རུས་ཐུག་པ་ཡིས།
ཡིད་ཆེས་གདེང་ཚད་འདི་འདྲ་བདོག་། གུས་པས་གསན་དང་སྐལ་བ་ཅན་། འཁོར་འདས་མ་རིག་གནས་ལུཌ་ལ་། གཟུང་འཛིན་ལྟ་བས་མ་བཅད་
ཅིང་། ངེས་ཤེས་ཉཾས་ཀྱིས་མ་བསླད་པར་། ཤེས་དང་ཤེས་བྱ་ཟད་པ་འདི་། ལྷག་མེད་རྟོཌ་པ་ལྟ་བའི་གདེང་། མ་བཅོས་ཐ་མལ་ཤེས་པ་འདི་། མ་
སྒོམ་སྙིང་གི་དབུས་སུ་སད་། ཚོཌ་དྲུག་སྣང་བ་རང་དགའ་དག་། དུས་གསུཾ་འདུ་འབྲལ་མེད་པ་འདི་། ཁོར་ཡུག་ཉཾས་མྱོང་སྒོམ་པའི་གདེང་། རྐྱེན་
སྣང་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་སྣ་ཚོཌ་ལ་། སྤོང་སྒྲུབ་གཉན་པོས་མ་བཅོས་པ་། རང་སར་རང་ཐོག་མཁན་པོ་ཟད་། ཞེན་འཛིན་རྩ་བ་འོལ་བ་འདི་། རྟུག་
ཕུད་རོ་སྙོམས་སྤྱོད་པའི་གདེང་། སེཾས་མེད་དཀར་ནག་ལས་ལས་གྲོལ་། སྣང་མེད་ཚོཌ་བརྒྱད་བརྟེན་པ་ཞིག་། ལུས་མེད་སྐྱེ་ཤིའི་འཇིཌ་དང་བྲལ་།
<leaf-break/>
ཐོན་། དོན་དམ་གཤིས་ཀྱི་གནས་ལུཌ་ལ་། ཡིད་ལ་བྱ་རུ་མི་བདོག་པས་། ཕྱོཌ་འཛིན་བལྟ་བའི་སྤྲོས་པ་ཆོད་། རང་ངོ་ཤེས་པ་ཟད་སར་སྐྱོལ་། ཡིན་ལུཌ་གཉུག་མའི་
རང་བབས་ལ་། བློ་ཡིས་སྒོམ་སྒྱུ་མི་གདའ་བས་། ཐ་མལ་ཤེས་པ་རྗེན་པར་ཞོག་། ཁ་ཡན་ཉཾས་མྱོང་བཟོ་མེད་སྐྱོངས་། རང་བྱུང་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་འདི་།
རི་ཁྲོད་སྤྱིལ་པོ་མ་ལུས་ཀྱི་། གང་ཤར་རང་ས་རང་ལ་ལྟོས་། སྣང་ཐོག་སྒོམ་གྱི་ཡང་རྩལ་སྦྱོངས་། ཡར་ལ་མོས་གུས་ས་སྡེ་ཚུཌ་། མར་ལ་ཚེ་འདི་
བརྡོས་ཐག་ཆོད་། བར་དུ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་བློ་སྣ་སྦྱོངས་། འབྲལ་མེད་རྟོཌ་པའི་རང་སྒོ་སྐྱོངས་། བརྟན་གཉེར་ཕྱག་ཆེན་བོཌ་འདོན་ཡིན་། གསུང་སྒྲུབ་འདི་ཕྱིའི་
ཏྲིལ་ཡིན་། བྱ་བྱེད་བླ་མའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཡིན་། ལས་སུ་མ་སྒོམ་ལཾ་དུ་སློངས་། སྐལ་ལྡན་ཡཾས་བཟང་པོ་ལ་། སྙིང་གཏཾ་ཉཾས་ལེན་གནས་
ལྔ་འདི་། བྱ་དགའ་ཡི་གེར་བསྐུར་བ་ཡིན་། སྙིང་གཏཾ་གནད་ལྔ་མ་ཨྠིི་། ་།ཨ་ནེ་འགག་མེད་ལ་གསུངས་སོ་། ་།ན་མོ་གུ་རུ། འགག་
མེད་སེཾས་ལ་འདི་ལྟར་ཞོག་། འཁོར་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བདེན་སྒྱུ་མེད་། ཚེ་སྲོག་མི་རྟག་འཆི་སར་སྙོགས་། ད་ལྟ་རྟྲཻལ་སྒྲིག་པ་ལ་། ཆོས་དང་སེཾས་
<leaf-break/>
རྟེན་མཆོག་དལ་འབྱོར་ཐོབ་པར་དཀའ། ཐོབ་དཀའི་མི་ཚེ་ཡེངས་ལ་ཟད། ངེས་མེད་འཆི་བས་རྟིང་ནས་ཐུག། ཤི་ནས་གར་སྐྱེས་རང་དབང་མེད། རྟཻལ་འཛོམ་
དུས་ཡུད་ཙམ་འདིར། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བསྐུལ་ཞིག་སྙིང་གཏཾ་ཡིན། འཁྲུལ་པའི་སྣང་བ་འབྱེད་པ་མཁས། གཏད་མེད་རིག་པ་མགོ་བཅོལ་ཆུང་། ངན་གོམས་

The late Lord, Vajradhara, stays forever in the hearts of embodied beings. Through the non-dual blessings of primordial wisdom, he accomplishes the ripening and liberation of the three times, equal to space. To the all-pervading Master of Great Bliss, I offer devotion in this time of inseparability. To the beggar, the cotton-clad yogi of the hermitage, by the kindness of the qualified Master, realization has reached the very marrow of the bone. I possess such confidence of conviction. Listen with respect, O fortunate ones. Regarding the mode of being of the state of ignorance in cyclic existence and nirvana: without being cut by the view of subject and object, and without being deceived by the experience of certain knowledge, this exhaustion of the knower and the knowable is the confidence of the view of realization without remainder. This unfabricated, ordinary awareness awakens in the center of the heart without meditation. This inseparability through the three times of the naturally pleasant appearances of the six collections <note>of consciousness</note> is the confidence of meditating on the experience of the continuous flow. Regarding the various objects of experience of appearing circumstances: without being fabricated by the antidotes of rejection or accomplishment, the Abbot who is on his own ground and on the spot is exhausted. This uprooting of the root of grasping and attachment is the confidence of the conduct of equal taste that takes the lead. One is liberated from the soulless karma of white and black. Relying on the eight collections where there is no appearance, one is free from the fear of bodiless birth and death. 
<leaf-break/>
Emerge! In the mode of being of the ultimate nature, since there is nothing to be done by the mind, cut through the elaborations of the view that holds to sides. Carry the recognition of your own face to the point of exhaustion. In the natural self-settling of the innate mode of being, since there is no meditation or cultivation by the intellect, leave ordinary awareness in its naked state. Sustain the unfabricated experience of being left to its own devices. Regarding this self-arisen Great Seal <term>Mahamudra</term>, in all the huts of the hermitages, look at whatever arises on its own ground. Train in the highest skill of meditation upon appearance. Above, establish the foundation of devotion. Below, cut the ties to the things of this life. In between, train the mindset of compassion. Sustain the own-door of inseparable realization. Stability and preservation are the enhancements of the Great Seal. The accomplishment of speech is the protector of this life and the next. The activities are the enlightened deeds of the Master. Do not meditate on them as work, but rouse them as the path. To the fortunate one with a good mind, these five points of heart-instruction practice are sent as a gift in writing. These are the five essential points of heart-instruction. Spoken to the nun Agme. Namo Guru. Let the mind remain in this way, unceasingly. There is no deceptive truth in the phenomena of cyclic existence. The life-force is impermanent and pursues the place of death. Regarding the current preparations, the Dharma and the mind—
<leaf-break/>
The supreme support, leisure and endowment, is difficult to obtain. This life, so hard to find, is wasted in distraction. Uncertain death arrives from behind. After dying, there is no self-control over where one is born. In this brief moment of the gathering of conditions, "Arouse diligence!" is my heart-advice. You are skilled at distinguishing the appearances of delusion. The undirected awareness has little focus. Habitual tendencies of bad habits are easily contracted. Turn the outward-looking mind toward the inside. Look at the reversal of the motivation and thoughts. "Let the mind and Dharma mix!" is my heart-advice. Regarding the false appearances that lack truth: through the illusory companionship of non-attachment, rely on the mindset of "whatever is pleasing" on the outer surface. Be satisfied with whatever happens and take it to the depths. Take hold of the immediate survival and the forward pursuit. "Be stubborn!" is my heart-advice. Toward the Master of the Body of Dharma <term>dharmakaya</term>, who possesses emptiness, generate measureless devotion. Toward the mother sentient beings of the six migrations, train the mindset in love and compassion. This complete and unmistakable excellent path—take hold of it from its essential points; that is my heart-advice. This unfabricated ordinary awareness—leave it on its own ground without meditating with the mind. Regarding the clarity of innate discursive thought, do not follow it, but look at that which dawns. In the all-encompassing Body of Dharma of appearance and existence, the antidote—

ལ། སྒོ་དང་རྟེན་གཞི་རྩོམ་ཚུལ་བསྟན་པ་དང་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་འཆད་པར་བཞེད་ནས། ཤིས་བརྗོད་ཕྱག་བྱ་དངོས་པོ་ནི། །ངེས་པར་བསྟན་པའང་དེ་ཡི་སྒོ། །དེ་ཡང་གཞུང་འདིའི་ཤིས་བརྗོད་རྒྱན་འཆད་སྐབས། མངོན་པར་འདོད་པའི་
དངོས་པོ་ལ། །སྨོན་པ་ཤིས་པ་བརྗོད་དེ་དཔེར། །ངག་གི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པའི། །སྣང་བ་དམ་པས་ཁྱོད་ལ་སྲུངས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་བཞིན། སྙན་ངག་གི་བསྟན་བཅོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་དཔག་བསམ་འཁྲི་ཤིང་གི་དབུར།
གང་ཐུགས་དྲི་བྲལ་ཤེལ་ལ་ཆགས་ཚོན་འཛིན་པ་མིན་པ་ཉིད། །ཡིད་ནི་སྙིང་རྗེས་བརླན་ལ་གང་གི་སྐྱོན་རྣམས་མ་ལུས་སྐམ། །གང་གིས་ཁྲོ་བ་མེད་ལ་རང་གི་འཁོར་བའི་དགྲ་མངོན་བཅོམ། །ཀུན་མཁྱེན་དེ་ཡིས་ཁྱེད་ལ་དགེ་ལེགས་གཡོ་བ་མེད་གྱུར་
ཅིག །ཅེས་བསྟན་བཅོས་ཀྱི་ཐོག་མར་ཤིས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་སྦྱོར་འགོད་པ་དང་། སྡེབ་སྦྱོར་རིན་ཆེན་འབྱུང་གནས་སུ། རྒྱལ་བ་ཐུབ་པ་ཉི་མ་ནི། །སྣང་བ་མཆོག་གི་བདག་ཉིད་ཅན། །ནང་གི་མཚན་མོ་ཤེས་བྲལ་གྱིས། །ནང་གི་ཉིན་བྱེད་ལ་
ཕྱག་འཚལ། །ཞེས་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟ་བུ་བསྟོད་ཡུལ་ལ་ཕྱག་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་འགོད་པ་དང་། མངོན་བརྗོད་སྣ་ཚོགས་གསལ་བ་ལས། །དེ་ནི་ཕུལ་བྱུང་སྙན་ངག་མཁན་གྱིས་ལམ་སྐྱེས་བརླིང་བ་ཅན། །བློ་ཡི་མིག་ལྡན་བླ་མས་བསྟན་པའི་མིག་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡི། །

"Those bound by the *Arya* and *Giti* <note>types of Sanskrit meter</note> are also Great Poetry." This is what is taught; in essence, that which investigates many occasions is Great Poetry. This is the meaning of "I shall explain its definition."
Second, regarding the actual definition, there are three parts: the entrance, the basis, and the method of composition. Intending to explain the first:
An auspicious expression, an act of homage, or the subject matter
Are certainly the entrance to that <note>Great Poetry</note>.
Furthermore, during the explanation of the "Ornament of Auspicious Expression" in this text, it says:
For the desired object,
An aspiration or auspicious expression is stated, for example:
"May the supreme light, which is not
The sphere of activity for speech, protect you."
As it is stated, at the beginning of the *Avadana-kalpalata* <gloss>A Wish-Fulfilling Vine of Noble Deeds</gloss>, the king of all poetic treatises:
"He whose mind does not take on the colors of passion upon the stainless crystal,
Whose heart is moistened by compassion and whose faults are entirely dried up,
Who is without anger and has visibly conquered the enemies of cyclic existence—
May that Omniscient One bring you unshakeable excellence!"
This is the placement of an auspicious composition at the start of a treatise. In the *Ratnakara* <gloss>Source of Jewels</gloss> <note>a treatise on Sanskrit prosody</note>:
"The Victorious Sage, the Sun,
Has the nature of the supreme light.
By the internal night, free of knowledge,
I bow to the internal Sun."
This is an example of placing words of homage to the object of praise. From the *Abhidhana-vishvaprakasha* <gloss>Manifestation of Various Synonyms</gloss>:
"By the various sublime poets, the path is made stable.
The Master who possesses the eyes of the intellect, who possesses the eye shown by the Guru..."
<leaf-break/>
...and achieving the physical objects of trade, jewels, and so forth through diligent enjoyment, and protecting what has been gathered.
The "Group of Desire" <term>kama-varga</term> is the engagement with the objects of the five senses <note>the qualities of desire</note> of gods, humans, and so forth, which are not the lower realms.
The "Group of Dharma" <term>dharma-varga</term> is the cause for the three higher rebirths <note>gods, demi-gods, and humans</note> and the three forms of enlightenment <note>shravaka, pratyekabuddha, and samyaksambuddha</note>; it is the infinite white dharmas <note>virtuous actions</note>.
The "Group of Liberation" <term>moksha-varga</term> is the enlightenment of the three vehicles which turns away from suffering and its causes.
The first two are concerned with cyclic existence; those who seek desire-objects achieve wealth as the cause for that. The latter two are concerned with the two types of Nirvana; seekers of liberation are diligent in achieving Dharma. Therefore, since these four are the essence of a person's aims and that which is to be achieved, they are "transformed" <note>into results</note> by those effects. In the *Jataka* <gloss>Birth Stories</gloss> they are called the "Three Groups," and in the *Ashtanga* <gloss>Eight Branches of Medicine</gloss>: "One should not rely on activities that lack the Three Groups, and one should not act in contradiction to them." This is it; the commentary explains that the dharma of liberation is included within the Group of Dharma.
Furthermore, it describes the lives of leaders of religion and politics <note>leaders of Dharma and the secular world</note> who are learned in the fields of knowledge such as the arts, and who possess extensive delightful qualities like noble birth, learning, and generosity. Examples include the *Avadana-kalpalata* <gloss>Wish-Fulfilling Vine of Noble Deeds</gloss> and the *Thirty-Four Birth Stories* <note>by Aryashura</note>, which tell the life stories of the Teacher, the Sugata.
<leaf-break/>
While it is clear that all conventional scholars do not accept anything other than the two—the "body" and the "ornament"—their habitual tendencies toward the science of healing have become powerful. As it is said: "Who would take up even a handsome human corpse that is not held by the life-faculty?" Thinking in this way, they consider it <note>life</note> necessary. However, since we see the arrangement of "beauty by ornaments" in many things that do not possess life—such as a chariot and the "ornament of a chariot," a divine palace and "its ornaments," or a gold belt "ornamented with jewels"—how can there be a certainty that one must correspond only to the three: a person's body, life, and ornaments? If it is certain that "body" requires "life," why are other faculties like eyes not also required? Furthermore, ornaments are neither beautiful nor appropriate on a naked person without clothes, so why say that? If one thinks that "life" is implied by "body," then why is "clothing" not also implied by "ornament"? Therefore, these various arguments result from being too attached to the analogy, turning what was clean into something messy.
The reason: Generally, "poetry" <term>kāvya</term> refers to words that are pleasant to the ear and captivate the mind. Within that, the "body" <term>śarīra</term> is the object, basis, or subject to be beautified by the composition of words, and the "ornaments" <term>alaṃkāra</term> are the terms for the qualities of the word-composition that make it beautiful. This is established by the two verses of the root text: "The body is the series of words, analyzed for the desired meaning," and "Those qualities that make poetry beautiful are called ornaments."

འཕྲེང་། །མཛེས་ལྡན་པདྨ་ཅན་གྱི་དཔལ་ཡོན་ཀུན། །སྙིང་སྡུག་འདི་ཡི་ལུས་ལ་ངེས་པར་གནས། །ངེས་པ་འགོག་པའི་སྦྱར་བ། ཕྱོགས་འདིར་སྲི་ལྡན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་མ་བགྲོད་པའི། །ལུས་ཕྲ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ལམ་རབ་སྟེར་བའི་མ། །
འོན་ཀྱང་མ་ངེས་སྐྱེ་མེད་མཚན་ལྡན་མའི། །སྔོ་སངས་ནམ་མཁའི་བུ་མོ་དག་ཀྱང་མཐོང་། །འགལ་མེད་ཀྱི་སྦྱར་བ། པདྨའི་སྐྱེ་གནས་ལ་བལྟམས་རང་བྱུང་གླུ། །འགྲོ་བའི་ཏོག་ཁྱོད་འཁོར་ལོས་ཕྱག་ཟུང་འབྲེལ། །འཆི་
མེད་དབང་ཕྱུག་བདུད་རྩི་སྤྲོ་བའི་ལྷ། །སྟེང་འཕུར་རྒྱལ་པོས་སུམ་རྩེན་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་འཇིགས། །འགལ་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྦྱར་བ་ནི། ཀུན་མཁྱེན་ཡིན་ཀྱང་རབ་ཆགས་ཀུན་རྟོགས་སྤངས། །མཁའ་འགྲོའི་དབང་ཕྱུག་ཡིན་ཀྱང་

༄༅། །སྐྱེ་བའི་མིག་སྔར་འཁྱེར་ལེགས་ཚུལ་ཆོས་ཁྲིམས། །ལས་འབྲས་མི་བསམ་ཁ་བཤད་སྐམ་པའི་ཆོས། །སྟོང་པོའི་ཚོན་གྱི་ལེགས་བྲིས་དབང་པོའི་གཞུ། །མཛེས་ཀྱང་ནམ་ཞིག་སྙིང་པོའི་རང་མཚང་སྟོད། །

བ་ནི། །ཐར་པ་འདོད་རྣམས་དྲི་མེད་ལ་སླ་བ་གཞིའི་རྒྱན། །སྙིང་ལ་སེམས་རྩུབ་དགའི་ལྟུང་བ་རྒྱས། །ལུས་མེད་ཕྱོགས་གྱུར་ནག་པོའི་རྩ་ལག་རྣམས། །དགའ་བའི་རྣམ་འགྱུར་རབ་སྤངས་སུ་འཛིན། །གཞི་གཅིག་པའི་
ཡོན་ཏན་འགལ་བ་ནི། ངེས་པར་རྣམ་བཀྲ་འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཚོགས། །ཚུར་དུ་དངར་བས་ཐར་པའི་བྱ་བ་ཉམས། །འཁྲུལ་པས་མ་བརྟགས་ཉམས་སུ་བདེ་བ་ཡི། །རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བའི་ཆོས་ནི་ཉིན་བཞིན་འཕེལ། །
རྫས་འགལ་བ་ནི། མགོ་སྐྱེས་རབ་ཏུ་དཀར་ཞིང་བཞིན་རས་སྔོ། །ཡན་ལག་གྱོང་ཡང་མྱོས་བྱེད་འཁྲི་ཤིང་མ་ཉེན། །ལུས་ཉིད་འཁྱོག་ཀྱང་རང་སེམས་དྲང་པོ་རུ། །སྲོང་བ་རྒན་པོའི་ལང་ཚོས་སུམ་བཅོམ། །རྫས་དང་
ལས་འགལ་བ་ནི། རྨ་བྱའི་མཇུག་སྒྲོའི་ཟུར་ཕུད་ཟླ་བའི་བཞིན། །པདྨའི་མཆུ་སྒྲོས་རྒྱུ་སྐར་འཕྲེང་བའི་ཚེམས། །རི་དགས་མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ལུས་ཕྲ་མས། །བདག་ཅག་འཁོར་བའི་མལ་དུ་ཅི་ཕྱིར་འཆིང་། །བྱ་བ་
<leaf-break/>
༄༅། །ཐུན་མོང་ཉིད་གྱུར་ནས། །ཅི་ཕྱིར་ཁྱོད་ཞབས་བསྟེན་ལས་སྨྲ་བ་ནི། །ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་པའི་ཁེངས་པ་འཛིན་རིགས་སམ། །སུམ་ཅུ་པ་ངེས་བསྟན་གྱི་རྒྱན་ལ། །དཔེ་ཡི་འཇུག་པས་དོན་དེ་ཉིད། །མཆོག་གམ་མཆོག་མིན་སྟོན་
པ་གཉིས། །ཞེས་པ་ལྟར་ལས། མཆོག་གི་ངེས་བསྟན་ནི། ངག་ལ་ངག་གི་དཔལ་སྟེར་དབྱངས་ལྷ་མོའི། །ཕངས་པར་རབ་མཛེས་ཤེལ་གྱི་ཏམྦུ་རར། །སེན་མོའི་སྟབས་བསྐྱེད་ཡིད་འོང་སྙན་སྒྲོགས་པ། །བརྩེ་བས་ཡོངས་བསྐུལ་ཆོས་
དོན་སྨྲ་བ་མཚོན། །མཆོག་ཡིན་ངེས་བསྟན་ནི། ལང་ཚོ་ལྡན་མ་དེ་ཡི་བྲང་གི་གཞིར། །རབ་རྒྱས་ནུ་མའི་ཤེལ་བུམ་ཟུང་མཛེས་པ། །སྲ་ཞིང་མཁྲེགས་པས་གང་གི་དབང་གྱུར་ལ། །ནམ་ཞིག་སྙིང་ཉིད་སྲ་བ་ངེས་པར་སྟོན། །སོ་གཅིག་
བལྟན་ཅིག་བརྗོད་པའི་རྒྱན་ལ། ཡོན་ཏན་ལས་རྣམས་ལྷན་ཅིག་བརྗོད། །གཞི་གཅིག་བྱ་བ་གཅིག་པ་སྟེ། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བརྗོད་པའི་དབྱེ་བ་གསུམ། །ཞེས་པ་ལྟར་ལས། ཡོན་ཏན་ལྷན་ཅིག་བརྗོད་པ་ནི། ལང་ཚོའི་དཔལ་ལས་
བྱུང་བའི་གཟི་མདངས་དང་། །ཡིད་འོང་པདྨ་གཞོན་ནུ་ལྷན་ཅིག་མཛེས། །གང་གི་བློ་དང་སྟོབས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་དང་། །དྲི་བཟང་ཁང་པའི་ཆུ་བ་ལྷན་ཅིག་བཀྲ། །ལས་ལྷན་ཅིག་བརྗོད་པ་ནི། ཀྱེ་མ་འབྱུང་འཁྲུགས་ནད་ཀྱི་ཟུག་རྔུ་
དང་། །ལྷན་ཅིག་རུས་ཚིགས་མདུད་པ་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱས། །ལུས་ཀྱི་ཉམས་བག་གཟི་མདངས་ཚོགས་རྣམས་དང་། །རྨོངས་པའི་གྲོགས་པོ་གཉིས་ནི་མཉམ་དུ་ཡལ། །བྱ་བ་ལྷན་ཅིག་བརྗོད་པ་ནི། སྲིད་པའི་སྐྱོན་གྱིས་རབ་བསྐྱེད་

<meta>continues from previous page: by the power of lying within the hearts of embodied beings, it clarifies the changes of movement and such born of the body</meta>... when the attachment to desire has completely faded, faith in the supreme source of merit greatly increases. 

The certain double-meaning <note>original: "niyata-śleṣa"</note> joined with saffron <note>original: "kesara"</note> and followed by *karkaṭaka* <gloss>white lotus</gloss>:
Adorned and based upon nectar, the garland of the twice-born <note>original: "dvija", meaning birds or brahmins</note>
And all the glorious qualities of the beautiful lotus-possessor <note>the lotus or a woman</note>
Certainly abide in the body of this beloved heart.

The restrictive negation double-meaning:
In this direction, the path of birth for the slender-bodied mother,
Where you, the lord of prosperity, have not traveled;
However, even the blue-green daughters of the sky,
The uncertain, unborn, and marked women, are seen.

The non-contradictory double-meaning:
Born in the lotus-birthplace, a self-arisen song;
You, the peak of beings, your two hands joined with the wheel;
The immortal lord, the deity who radiates nectar;
The king flying above terrifies the city of the thirty-three <note>the realm of the gods</note>.

The contradictory double-meaning is:
Though he is the All-Knowing <note>the Buddha</note>, he abandoned all concepts of great attachment.
Though he is the Lord of the Sky-Goers <note>Ḍākinīs</note>, he is compassionate toward the earth-goers <note>snakes</note>.
He is a *Śabara* <gloss>mountain hunter</gloss>, yet he does not kill the supreme bull.
Though he is a deity himself, he is designated as a "traveler" <note>wandering being</note>.

The twenty-fifth is the Ornament of Specific Description <note>original: "viseṣokti-alaṃkāra"</note>. It has five types: describing the specific qualities, types, actions, substances, and causes.
The description of specific qualities where a quality is lacking:
Your method, O you who possess the conduct of purity,
Is neither hard, nor firm, nor thick.
Even so, no matter how many weapons the one with the flower bow <note>Kāmadeva, the god of love</note>
Has let fall, the vessel...

<leaf-break/>

...one who carries before the eyes of birth the excellent way of the Dharma laws.
Dry talk of Dharma without contemplating karma and its results,
Is like the Indra’s bow <gloss>rainbow</gloss> well-drawn with empty colors;
Though beautiful, one day the true nature of its core will be exposed.

The twenty-seventh is the Ornament of Contradiction <note>original: "virodha-alaṃkāra"</note>. As it is said:
Contradictory actions with different bases,
Two qualities contradicting in one base,
Contradiction of substances, contradiction of substance and action,
Contradiction of actions, and contradiction of double-meanings—these are the six.
Regarding contradictory actions with different bases:
Those who desire liberation follow the stainless path <note>this is the ornament of the easy base</note>;
Harsh thoughts in the heart cause the fall from joy to flourish.
The bodiless ones <note>desires/emotions</note> who have become partial and the dark-sided relatives,
Abandon the expressions of joy and hold to them as such.

The contradiction of qualities in a single base:
The collection of desired qualities is certainly diverse;
By being arranged here, the activities of liberation are impaired.
The phenomena of distraction, which are pleasant when not examined through confusion,
Increase day by day.

The contradiction of substances:
The hair on the head is very white, yet the face is blue.
The limbs are stiff, yet the intoxicating vine was not touched.
The body itself is crooked, yet the mind is made straight;
The youth of an old man is conquered by the three <note>referring to the three times or three ailments</note>.

The contradiction of substance and action:
A face like the moon with the crest of a peacock's tail feather,
Lips like a lotus and teeth like a string of stars;
Why does the slender-bodied woman with the eyes of a deer
Bind us in the bed of cyclic existence?

The contradiction of action...

<leaf-break/>

...having become common,
Why should the speech arising from serving your feet
Be held with the pride of having become great?

The thirtieth is the Ornament of Definitive Indication <note>original: "yathāsaṃkhya-alaṃkāra"</note>:
Through the application of examples, the meaning itself
Is shown as either supreme or not supreme—these are the two.
The definitive indication of the supreme:
The Sarasvatī <note>Goddess of Speech</note> who bestows the glory of speech upon speech;
On the crystal lute <term>tambura</term> so beautiful in her lap,
She produces delightful, sweet sounds with the movement of her nails;
Completely urged by compassion, she illustrates the speech on the meaning of Dharma.

The definitive indication of the non-supreme <note>text says "supreme", likely a continuation of the category</note>:
On the foundation of the chest of that youthful woman,
The beautiful pair of crystal-vase breasts is fully swollen;
Because they are firm and hard, whoever falls under their power,
One day it is definitively shown that the heart itself is hard.

The thirty-first is the Ornament of Simultaneous Description <note>original: "sahokti-alaṃkāra"</note>:
Describing qualities and actions together,
One base with one action;
These are the three divisions of simultaneous description.
The simultaneous description of qualities:
The radiance arising from the glory of youth
And the delightful young lotus are beautiful together.
The nature of one’s intellect and strength
And the water of the fragrant chamber are bright together.

The simultaneous description of actions:
Alas, the piercing pain of the disease of shifting elements
Increases together with the knots of the bone joints.
The collection of the body’s vitality and radiance
And the two friends of ignorance vanish together.

The simultaneous description of activities:
Greatly produced by the faults of existence...

འདི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྟེ། མཉམ་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ། །མཉམ་པ་ཞེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། སྦྱོར་བ་སྟེ་བརྩམས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ལ་གང་ཞིག་ཐོག་མཐའ་བར་རྣམས་སུ་རྐང་པ་བཞི་ཀ་ལའང་མི་མཉམ་

Among those who belong to the various directions, this path of poetry has arisen. Even by saying this, it is clear that the desire of the Easterners is for both the former and latter actual examples shown. However, according to the Indian commentary by Master Ratnashri, it occurs as follows: To definitively show the nature of evenness, it says, that which is called evenness, and so forth. In the domain of compositions—that is, the arrangements—where there is no unevenness in any of the four lines at the beginning, end, or middle, and they are arranged in a consistent and equal manner, that should be known as even poetry. Thus it is said. If one asks by how much those arrangements become uneven or even, it says, that is, and so forth. Those arrangements occur in three types: soft, harsh, and intermediate. Evenness refers to being supple and relaxed, because being relaxed and supple is the opposite of being constricted. As it was said: As much as what was previously heard as soft. Harshness is hearing an excess of aspirated sounds, because difficulty of expression is the opposite of extreme youthfulness. As it says: The characteristics that will be explained, and so forth. Mixed is hearing what is intermediate. Again, if one asks what the source of these is, it says soft, and so forth. Soft refers to those sounds heard softly, such as the letter Ka and others. The occurrence of harshness is an excess of aspirates.

<leaf-break/>

The southern Malaya breeze, which has been washed and become cool, will come near and meet me. This should be how it is arranged. This is uneven because it mixes inconsistent types, being half soft and half harsh. In this very case, by filling out and arranging two half-verses of consistent types, there would be an arrangement of entirely soft sounds and an arrangement of entirely harsh sounds; there would be two verses, and by that, they should be understood as examples of evenness. This is what occurs. For that reason, in the *Condensed Commentary* composed by the Omniscient Pema Karpo, it says: Here, the former was interpreted to mean that if a line is small, it is evenly small; if intermediate, evenly intermediate; and if large, evenly large. The latter implies that if all—large, small, and intermediate—exist in each line equally, it is even. Other commentators explain differently, but that does not appear to be correct. Furthermore, some say that even for the Easterners, if the sounds are uneven, there must still be an equality of meaning. Without that, it would not even receive the name "evenness." The name must exist consistently across the ten paths. For the sake of accomplishment, the cause produces the effect, or the definition properly establishes the subject to be defined. By the result of that—possessing the flavor and experience of excellence in both word and meaning—just as those who use honey—that is, as bees are made joyful by honey—likewise, the wise poets who know the experience of poetry are made joyful and satisfied by it. For that reason, in the Indian commentary by Master Ratnashri, it occurs at this point as follows: To explain the expansion of sweetness, it says "sweetness" and so forth; by saying that which possesses the experience of poetry, it expresses sweetness. Again, if one asks what that possession of experience is like, it possesses sweetness in both sound and meaning. To show that kind of form, it says "words" and so forth; "words" refers to the sound. "Object" refers to the meaning. The experience resides in both; this is the meaning of possessing the experience of sweetness in both. If one asks what that does, it says "by which" and so forth. སེངྒེ་ཡོད་པའི་ལུང་གི་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་ལ། རྒྱ་གར་བའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་རྣམས་ནས་ཧ་རི་ན་ཐཿསྟེ་མགོན་འཕྲོག་ཏུ་གྲགས་པའི་རི་དྭགས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་བྱང་ཐང་དུ་གནས་པ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པར་གྲགས་པ་ལས། གཞན་འདམ་སེང་དུ་གྲགས་
པ་ཞིག་ཀྱང་ཡོད་པའི་ཁུངས་མ་མཐོང་བས་བརྟག་པར་བྱ་བའི་གནས་སུ་སྣང་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །གཉིས་པ་དུས་འགལ་གྱི་དཔེར་བརྗོད། པདྨ་ཅན་ནི་མཚན་མོ་རྒྱས། །ཉིན་བར་ཀུ་མུཏ་ལྡན་པ་གསལ། །དཔྱིད་ནི་ནི་ཙུ་ལ་རབ་རྒྱས། །
སོས་ཀ་དག་ནི་སྤྲིན་གྱིས་གཏིབས། །ངང་པའི་སྒྲ་ནི་དབྱར་མཉན་འོས། །སྟོན་ནི་རྨ་བྱ་མྱོས་པ་སྟེ། །དགུན་སྟོད་ཉི་མ་དྲི་མ་མེད། །དགུན་ནི་ཙནྡན་བསྔགས་པར་འོས། །ཞེས་པ་འདི་འདྲ་དུས་དང་ནི། །འགལ་བའི་ལུགས་དག་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན། །
པདྨ་ཅན་ཏེ་པདྨའི་སྡོང་བུ་ནི་མཚན་མོ་རྒྱས་པས་དེའི་མེ་ཏོག་ཁ་བྱའོ་ཅེས་པ་དང་། ཉིན་པར་ཀུ་མུཏ་ལྡན་པ་སྟེ་ཀུ་མུ་ཏའི་སྡོང་པོ་གསལ་ཞིང་རྒྱས་པས་དེའི་མེ་ཏོག་ཀྱང་གསལ་ལོ་ཞེས་པའི་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་པོ་འདི་ཉིན་མཚན་གྱི་གནས་
ལུགས་དང་འགལ་བའོ། །སྐབས་འདིར་འགྲེལ་པ་རྣམས་སུ་པདྨ་ཅན་ཉི་མ་དང་། ཀུ་མུཏ་ལྡན་པ་ཟླ་བ་ལ་ངོས་བཟུང་ཡང་དེའི་བཤད་ཁུངས་མེད། རྒྱ་འགྲེལ་ནས་ཀྱང་སྔར་དོན་གཞན་བཀོད་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་པདྨོ་ཅན་ནི་པདྨའི་ཚལ་དང་།

༄༅། །བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་པའི་རྐང་པ་སྔ་མ་གཉིས་འདིར་འགྱུར་བཅོས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་ལེགས་ཏེ། གཞུང་གི་རྒྱ་དཔེར། སྠཱ་ཡི་ཞེས་འབྱུང་བ་བོད་སྐད་གནས་ཅན་ཏེ་ཉམས་བརྒྱད་པོའི་སྤྱི་མིང་དང་། དེ་ཡང་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པ་
ལུས་ངག་ཏུ་མ་ཐོན་ཅིང་། ཡིད་ཀྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་ཀུན་སློང་ཐོག་མའི་ས་བོན་ལྟ་བུར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ལ་ཡིད་བྱེད་དམ་གནས་ཞེས་བྱ། དེ་ཆེས་ཆེར་འཕེལ་བས་ལུས་ངག་གི་ཉམས་འགྱུར་རོ་ཉམས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པ་ལ་ཉམས་སམ་
གནས་ཅན་ཞེས་བྱ། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་གནས་སམ་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པ་རེ་དང་། གནས་ཅན་ནམ་ཉམས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་འབྲས་བུར་གྱུར་པ་རེ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་སུ་འབྲེལ་བའི་འབྲེལ་པ་མ་འཆོལ་བར་འབྱུང་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར། འདིར་
ཡང་སྤྲོ་བའི་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གནས་འཕེལ་བ་དཔའ་བའི་གནས་ཅན་ནམ་ཉམས་དང་། དགའ་བའི་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གནས་འཔེལ་བ་ལས་སྒེག་པའི་ཉམས་སམ་གནས་ཅན་དག་བྱུང་བ་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁྲོ་བའི་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གནས་འཔེལ་
བ་དྲག་པོའི་ཉམས་སམ་གནས་ཅན་དང་། ཡ་མཚན་པའི་གནས་སམ་ཡིད་བྱེད་འཕེལ་བ་རྨད་བྱུང་གི་གནས་ཅན་ནམ་ཉམས་ཞེས་སྨོས་དགོས་པ་ལ། འདིར་དཔའ་བའི་ཡིད་ཀྱི་གནས་ཅན་ཁྲོ་བ་དང་། སྒེག་པའི་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་
གནས་ཅན་ཡ་མཚན་ནོ་ཅེས་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་དང་། ཡང་དབྱངས་བདུན་ནི་དྲང་སྲོང་དང་། ས་འཛིན་དང་། དྲུག་སྐྱེས་དང་། བར་མ་དང་། བློ་གསལ་དང་། ལྔ་པ་དང་། འཁོར་ཉན་རྣམས་ཏེ་དེ་བདུན་ཀ་གཅིག་ཏུ་རྫོགས་ཤིང་འདྲེས་པ་དེ་སྙན་

༄༅། །པའམ། ཡང་ན་སྒྱུ་རྩལ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡོངས་སུ་བཅད་པ་གོམས་པར་གྱུར་པ་ལས་རང་རང་གི་གནས་ལུགས་སམ་རང་བཞིན་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །བཞི་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་དང་འགལ་བའི་དཔེར་བརྗོད་ནི། །
གླང་པོ་དག་ནི་རལ་པོ་གཡོ། །རྟ་ཡི་རྭ་ནི་རྣོ་བ་ཡིན། །ཨེ་རཎྜ་ནི་སྙིང་པོ་ལྕི། །སེང་ལྡེང་ལྗོན་པ་སྙིང་པོ་མེད། །ཅེས་པ་འདི་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་པ། །ཉིད་དང་འགལ་བ་ཀུན་གྱིས་སྨད། །གླང་པོ་ཆེ་ལ་རལ་པ་གཏན་ནས་མེད་པ་ལ་དེ་གཡོའོ་ཞེས་པ་དང་།
རྟ་ལ་རྭ་མེད་པ་ལ་དེ་རྣོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་དག་ནི་གཡོ་བ་བཅུད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་གནས་ལུགས་དང་འགལ་བ་ཡིན་ལ། སྐབས་འདིར་དཔང་ཊཱིཀ་ཏུ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སེངྒེ་ལ་གཡུ་རལ་ཡོད་དོ་ཅེས་པའང་སྟེ་འདུལ་བ་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་དུ། སེངྒེའི་སྐྲ་་་
སེར་སྐྱར་གསུངས་པས་སོ། །ཞེས་པ་ལ། ཡང་རྗེ་བོད་མཁས་པས་སྔ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་སེངྒེ་ལ་རིགས་མང་བས་སྐྲ་ཡང་གཅིག་ལས་སེར་སྐྱར་བཤད་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཁྱབ་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཀྱང་སེངྒེ་ལ་རིགས་མང་བ་དང་།
དེའི་བྱེ་བྲག་འགའ་ཞིག་ལ་གཡུ་རལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཁུངས་ཀྱང་བཙལ་ན་རྙེད་སླ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཅིང་། དོན་དུ་ནི་སེངྒེའི་གཡུ་རལ་ཟེར་བ་འདི་བོད་ཡུལ་ན་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས། རྒྱ་གར་ན་སེངྒེ་རལ་དམར་ཅན་ཟེར་བ་ཡིན། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཨེ་རཎྜ་ཏེ་དན་རོག་
གི་ཤིང་ནི་བོད་ཀྱི་ལྕིམ་ལྟ་བུ་སྲ་མཁྲེགས་ཅི་ཡང་མེད་པ་ལ་སྙིང་པོ་ལྕི་ཞེས་པ་དང་། སེང་ལྡེང་གི་ལྗོན་པ་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་སྲ་ཞིང་མཁྲེགས་པའི་ཚད་དུ་བརྩི་བ་ལ་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་ཅེས་སྨོས་པ་སྟེ། རྐང་པ་ཕྱི་མ་འདི་གཉིས་ནི་བརྟན་པ་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་

...although the fame of the "snow lion" is true, that was spoken without investigation by following the long-standing fame among the elders of Tibet who had little knowledge of those lands. Therefore, it does not serve as scriptural proof for lions existing on snow mountains. In Indian treatises, there is a specific type of deer known as <term>harinatha</term> <gloss>Lord of Deer</gloss> famous for dwelling on the northern plains, but no source has been seen for the existence of what is famous as a "swamp lion." Thus, it appears to be a point for investigation, he said.

The lotus-pool blooms at night,
The water-lily is clear during the day.
In spring, the <term>nicula</term> <gloss>cane</gloss> blooms profusely,
The summer is covered by clouds.
The sound of geese should be heard in summer,
In autumn, the peacocks are intoxicated.
In early winter, the sun is stainless,
In winter, sandalwood is worthy of praise.
Such as these are the traditions
Taught to be in contradiction with time.
"The lotus-pool" means the lotus stalk blooms at night and its flowers open, and "the water-lily is clear during the day" means the water-lily stalk is clear and blooming and its flowers are also clear; these two lines contradict the natural state of day and night. In this context, the commentaries identify "lotus-pool" with the sun and "water-lily" with the moon, but there is no source for that explanation. Even in the Sanskrit commentary, when previously establishing "other-meaning-setting," the "lotus-pool" was a grove of lotuses...

<leaf-break/>

...it will become. The two previous lines are better if revised here as they were. In the Sanskrit text of the treatise, <term>sthāyi</term> appears, which in Tibetan is "stable-possessor" <gloss>enduring emotion</gloss>, the general name for the eight aesthetic flavors. Also, that which has not emerged into body or speech as its cause, but exists as a primary seed-like motivation of the state of mind, is called "mental engagement" or "base." When that increases greatly and becomes possessed of the flavor of physical and verbal aesthetic expressions, it is called "flavor" <gloss>rasa</gloss> or "stable-possessor." Because a specific "base" or "mental engagement" as the cause and a specific "stable-possessor" or "flavor" as the result must occur without confusing their causal relationship, here too: from the increase of the base of "enthusiasm" comes the stable-possessor or flavor of "heroism," and from the increase of the base of "delight" comes the flavor or stable-possessor of "eroticism." Similarly, from the increase of the base of "anger" comes the flavor or stable-possessor of "wrath," and from the increase of the base of "wonder" comes the flavor or stable-possessor of "marvel." Instead of stating it thus, to say "the stable-possessor of the heroic mind is anger" and "the stable-possessor of the erotic mental engagement is wonder" is <note>the fault</note>. 
Also, the seven musical notes are: <term>rishabha</term> <gloss>Sage/Bull</gloss>, <term>gandhara</term> <gloss>Mountain-holder</gloss>, <term>shadja</term> <gloss>Six-born</gloss>, <term>madhyama</term> <gloss>Middle</gloss>, <term>dhaivata</term> <gloss>Clear-mind</gloss>, <term>panchama</term> <gloss>Fifth</gloss>, and <term>nishada</term> <gloss>Outcaste-listener</gloss>. That all seven are complete and blended together is...

<leaf-break/>

...or else, from the familiarity of the definitions of the arts, their own natural state or suchness will become clear. 
Fourth, the examples of "contradiction with the world":
Elephants have swaying manes,
The horns of a horse are sharp.
The <term>eranda</term> <gloss>castor</gloss> has a heavy core,
The <term>khadira</term> <gloss>acacia</gloss> tree has no core.
This is contradiction with the world
Itself, and is despised by all.
To say an elephant "sways its mane" when it has no mane at all, and to say a horse's "horns are sharp" when it has no horns, contradicts the natural state of the moving world of sentient beings. In this context, Pang's Commentary says: "Likewise, to say a lion has a turquoise mane; for the *Vinaya-vibhasha* states a lion's hair is pale yellow." Regarding this, Master Bod Mkhas Pa says, as before, since there are many species of lions, the explanation of one as pale yellow does not pervade all. However, it is not easy to find a source for there being many species of lions or for certain types having turquoise manes. In fact, what is called a "turquoise mane" is famously known in Tibet; in India, it is said lions have "red manes." Similarly, the <term>eranda</term> or castor tree is like the Tibetan <term>chim</term> <gloss>shrub</gloss>, having no hardness or solidity, so to say its "core is heavy," and to say the <term>khadira</term> tree, which is considered the standard of extreme hardness and solidity, has "no core," are contradictions. These last two lines contradict the stable world of the environment...
